title: A note in the searcher's pocket
allegory: An S-inhibition head is a colleague who slips a note into the searcher's pocket saying 'skip John, he came up twice', so when the name mover scans the sentence for a name to fetch, it passes over John and fetches Mary.

chapters.name: Who gets the drink?
chapters.note: Mary ... obviously. But how does it know?

props.label: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to ___

cap.1: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to... Mary, obviously. But a model has to work out which name not to say.
cap.2: GPT-2 small completes the IOI prompt with ' Mary'. Copying a name is easy for attention; knowing which of the two names to avoid needs extra machinery.
cap.3: Attending to two copies of John looks like attending to one, so counting is awkward for attention. The IOI circuit instead flags the repeated subject and suppresses it.

props.label: skip John: he came up twice

cap.1: At the end of the sentence, a searcher is about to fetch a name. A colleague hurries over with a note: 'skip John, he came up twice.' So it fetches Mary.
cap.2: S-inhibition heads in layers 7 and 8 carry a 'this name is duplicated' flag to the final position. The name movers read it there and avoid John.
cap.3: Heads 7.3, 7.9, 8.6 and 8.10 move the flag from S2 to END; name movers 9.6, 9.9 and 10.0 then attend from END to the indirect object and copy it.

cap.1: A relay: one part spots the repeat, the S-inhibition heads carry the warning to the end, and the searchers use it to fetch the right name.
cap.2: Duplicate-token heads flag S2 as a repeat. S-inhibition heads move that flag to END. Name movers attend to the name that is not flagged and copy it.
cap.3: S-inhibition heads read the flag through their values (V-composition) and write into the name movers' queries (Q-composition). Patching their values changes the answer; their keys mostly do not.

chapters.name: Pocket, not sign

right.title: sign over John (key)
lines: patch into keys, values: much less

chapters.verdict: The inhibition arrives in the name movers' queries, not their keys.

cap.1: The note goes in the searcher's pocket; nobody hangs a sign on John. What changes is what the searcher looks for, not how John looks.
cap.2: Path patching from each head into the name movers' queries lights up the S-inhibition heads; into their keys and values, much less. The signal is a query.
cap.3: Activation patching alone cannot separate these routes. Path patching isolates the edge into the queries of 9.6, 9.9 and 10.0, establishing Q-composition over K- or V-composition.

chapters.name: Flip the right name
chapters.verdict: Before corrupting a prompt, list every clue the model could use.

cap.1: The searcher can find Mary two ways: by her name, or by which chair she sat in. Swap names carelessly and only one clue flips: a muddled test.
cap.2: The model locates the indirect object by token and by position. Flipping all three names reverses only the token signal, so patching results smear. Flip only S1.
cap.3: A corrupted distribution must reverse every signal you care about. Flipping only S1 moves the indirect object's token and position signals together, a clean contrast for patching.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Knowing where not to look is a job
Found by path patching, not pictures

cap.1: Some parts of a model do not produce answers; they steer other parts away from wrong ones. Finding those vetoes is part of understanding a model.
cap.2: The S-inhibition heads were found by causal intervention, and their query route only by path patching. That is the standard for any circuit claim you make.
cap.3: Suppressive, query-side signals are how circuits compose a decision. When you set out to steer a behaviour, the vetoes are handles too, not only the parts that write the answer.

coda.title: Knock out S-inhibition heads and watch where the searcher looks (toy)

params.label: how firmly each note says 'skip John'

readouts.label: prediction
readouts.f: (a => a[0] > a[1] + 0.05 ? 'Mary' : (a[1] > a[0] + 0.05 ? 'John' : 'a coin flip'))(softmax([1, 1 - heads*push]))

caption.1: Knock out S-inhibition heads one by one, or weaken their notes. Watch the searcher's attention slide from Mary back to a coin flip between the names.
caption.2: With no inhibition the name mover likes both names equally and the prediction is a coin flip. Each head's note lowers John's score from the query side.
caption.3: Toy: score(John) = 1 - heads·push inside the name mover's QK, softmax over the two names. Real heads differ in strength, and the rest of the circuit is ignored here.

where_else: Name mover heads, which do the copying once told where not to look
Path patching, the method that showed the signal enters as a query
Negative name movers 10.7 and 11.10, parts that push the other way
Q-composition in general: one head reshaping what a later head searches for

hamming.what: Middle-layer heads that carry a 'this name is repeated' flag to the end of the sentence so the name movers avoid it.
hamming.when: In GPT-2 small's IOI circuit, layers 7 and 8, whenever a sentence repeats the subject's name.
hamming.why: They show a circuit can work by telling other parts where not to look, and that the route (queries, not keys) matters as much as the component.

object.title: The relay tower
object.subtitle: Four words on the floor, three kinds of worker above; follow the flag from the repeated name to the answer.

cap.1: Four words on the floor, three kinds of worker above. Follow the glow from the repeated John up to the last word.
cap.2: Token positions along the bottom; heads stacked by layer above the positions where they act.
cap.3: IOI prompt, ABBA template: IO, S1, S2, END. Heads are placed at the destination position they write to.

cap.1: First stop: at the second John, a head notices it has seen this name before and writes a flag.
cap.2: Duplicate-token heads at S2 attend back to S1 and write 'this token is a repeat'.
cap.3: The flag says only 'duplicated', with no identity or position information; path patching shows the S-inhibition keys read a little of it (a residual K-composition).

cap.1: The S-inhibition heads at the last word read that flag and carry it over: information moved, not attention redirected.
cap.2: They attend from END to S2 and copy the flag through their values: V-composition.
cap.3: Patching S-inhibition values changes the answer, patching their keys mostly does not: evidence for V- over K-composition.

cap.1: The flag lands in the name movers' question, so they look past John and fetch Mary to the output.
cap.2: The S-inhibition output enters the name movers' queries, suppressing attention to S and leaving the IO to copy.
cap.3: Q-composition into W_Q of 9.6, 9.9, 10.0, established by path patching; the IO is then copied to the logits through their OV circuits.

cap.1: Not every worker helps: some late heads push toward John. The answer is a tug of war that Mary wins.
cap.2: Negative name movers 10.7 and 11.10 write against the right answer; 10.7 alone makes the wrong logit about 7x more likely.
cap.3: Circuits are net effects of competing components, and the negative movers' function is still not settled.

predict.q: Where does the S-inhibition signal enter the name movers?
predict.why: Path patching into the name movers' queries lights up the S-inhibition heads; their keys and values show much less.

predict.q: You patch the S-inhibition heads' values, then their keys. Which changes the answer more?
predict.why: They move a flag (V-composition). Patching their keys mostly does nothing, though path patching finds a small K-composition.

predict.q: With every S-inhibition head knocked out, what would the name movers lack?

options.t: The ability to copy a name at all

predict.why: The name movers do the copying; the S-inhibition heads only tell them where not to look.

object.where: Any relay where one part tells another where not to look, carried in the question rather than on the target.
